payload.reference: docs/studies/round-36/sheet.png (provisional — built from the brain dumps, not user-picked)

open: the Info tab is one long card; Start over sits at the bottom of it
the container yard sits close under the ship HUD at 390 wide
the gantry and W19's catch tower overlap as two lattices at the same spot
coast time-lapses past tier 8
sun is fixed at upper-left; does not parallax
the flaps are flat slabs — they read at a glance but have no thickness or hinge travel
the gimbal HUD covers the grandstand during the catch on a phone
the cargo scene runs 46 fps headless (every other scene 61) — fill rate, not draw count: any one large translucent element removed puts it back over 60
ten equipment cards make a long scroll on a phone
the priciest strategy still waits 18 launches at its worst — the longest hold in the game
the tier-9+ nose beacon does not pulse while the stack is apart (the slices are blits from a per-tier bake)
the VAB deliberately runs off the left edge; on a phone the high bay and the fuelling hall show, the office floors do not
the recovery flaps are drawn side-on only; edge-on there is nothing to see
countdown numerals sit over the crane boom on desktop
flight is 10–21 s per mission; the hour-long game is T14
the cross-fade from the pad view still overlaps the first second of the lap, so a large pad rocket sits over the globe while the small one is already in orbit
the cargo payoff panel still overlaps the Earth lobe low on a phone, where it wraps to five lines
at 390 wide the site is dense — everything is there and readable, but it is a lot
drawLife's golf cart passes in front of the container yard's back fence at the far-left end of its lap, two frames per lap
the visitor plaza still has its bottom-right corner under the LAUNCH button in portrait
the 'ascent' curve is invented — no pad-scene ship position lines up with it yet, so it is unused
a true circle never crosses the Moon’s disc, so the far half is told by the fade alone — there is no hard occlusion any more
the whole game is now 43-106 launches, down from 113-176 — the 10-launch endgame necessarily removed the old tail, and the mid-game has not been re-lengthened to compensate

payload.note: Pitch-over and the camera ladder (T13c/T15/T16/T30/T31). A flight is now a phase machine: ascent (physics replay) → gravity turn → Earth orbit → dotted transfer arc → lunar orbit → cargo drop → return → parachute, cross-fading between camera views so each mission zooms out one step and the Moon zooms back in. Budgets per mission: 10 s at mission 1, 21 s for the full Moon round trip, under the 30 s cap. The ladder re-scales: altitude, then distance to the Moon, then population toward 10,000. Zero console errors, 60–61 fps, sim PASS. T33/T34/T24: the readiness window owns the top-left on the ground and becomes a go/no-go board when idle; mission control and the gimbal take over the moment the flight starts. Task pool is 36 jokey items grouped into six assembly stages, read as live commentary. T35 optimization: static farm and pad layers cached to offscreen canvases, fills batched, off-screen ground culled. Pad 150 draws to 49, turnaround 232 to 140, desktop turnaround 55 fps to 61. Verified identical with the clock frozen: 0.06% of pixels differ, none by more than 64/255, all on cached-layer antialiasing seams. T14 retune: cost growth 2.55, equipment priced above the tier it unlocks, population 0.95 per tonne. A player who buys what they can afford reaches low Earth orbit on launch 14 and finishes in about an hour. T17 railgun: fires during the Moon cargo phase where the camera actually is, pays about 90 cents per resident, grows with the colony. T36–T39 + A1/A2: ten mishaps, the upper-right checklist, a square LAUNCH with its own clock, the rocket lifting off the pad, and one canonical journey geometry — Earth lower-left, counter-clockwise orbit, a lunar orbit at the Moon. T40 then moved the figure eight to where Apollo puts it: it spans the whole Earth-Moon path — a long lobe past the Earth, a tight hook round the far side of the Moon, crossing between them — while the Moon itself gets a circular orbit, and the return leg runs forward round the second half instead of rewinding the first. T52 fixed the one thing a ballistic object cannot do: the ship used to snap upright the instant the engine quit. It now carries its burnout lean on round the arc — horizontal at the top, nose-down on the way back — and the descent splits into two rates so the canopy has time to read. Under the chute the ship turns about the riser above it rather than its own base, so it hangs as weight on a line and its swing damps out; the pitch instrument reads the same attitude the player can see. T53/T55/T56: the parachute is gone from the game. The ship swings its recovery flaps out in thick air, belly-flops flat to the airstream, flips to vertical between 9 and 4 km, lights the engine at 7 km and is taken by the chopsticks under 3 km — drawCatch's drogue removed with the rest. T54 moved the payoff panel out of the middle of the frame, where it covered the catch, into the right column under the to-do box, positioned from the measured goal window and carrying a tonnes-and-$/tonne line. The green aurora is deleted. Building the flaps turned up T56: the W1 rocket block was in the file twice and the later, plainer copy won every call, so drawRocket's opts — heat, cargo bay — had never rendered. One definition now. T57: the cloud deck fades out below 13 km on the way down and is gone by 10, so the flip, the landing burn and the catch play against clear sky — the climb still flies through it. T58: each shop tab carries one green dot per upgrade that is unlocked and affordable right now, so a glance says where the money can go. T59 re-shot the orbit view: the camera now looks down on the plane rather than along it, so the ring is a tall ellipse whose top half runs behind the globe. The lap runs counter-clockwise from the top right — the ship leaves behind the Earth and comes around to the front. A low-orbit flight has nowhere to go, so it makes a full lap and a half round to the lower left, holds station, turns end-for-end and burns retrograde to come down; a Moon mission keeps its shorter three-quarter staging lap to the transfer corner and never flips. The ring lives in one helper, orbitRing, that drawOrbitView and the dotted trajectory overlay both read. T60-T64 and T67: the free-return eight no longer kinks at its crossing (lobe sizes blended on cos t rather than switched — 18.4° worst turn to 0.78°); the ladder carries plain-English station names under each code; a milestone is credited on touchdown so the checklist holds the mission you are flying until you are home; the shop's "buy the two items below" line is gone; the chopstick catch owns the last 38% of the descent and runs 1.55 s instead of 0.7; and the lunar orbit is a true circle concentric with the Moon rather than a squashed tipped oval. T65/T66 rebuilt the ground. The turnaround left the pad: the booster is set on a crawler, ferried across the site and back in through the open front of a cutaway VAB two and a half times the old hangar's height, taken apart nose-first, worked on across three platform levels, put back together and rolled out — ten beats over the same 10 s, on the existing checklist stages. The site around it doubled: industrial estate behind the rocket, farm and pond moved right, grandstand at bottom centre with the front road gone, an open-fence warehouse with lorries cycling through three dock bays, an ADMIN building where the fuel farm was, helipad far right, a grass concourse, and 17 live events. The VAB is drawn live rather than into the cached site layer because it is sized from S.tiers and the cache key does not know them. T68 was a real bug: buy() and buyEquip() never called paintGauges, so PAYLOAD and REVENUE — the two numbers the flight plan exists for — only caught up after the next launch. T70: the admin staff were not moving to any eye (3.7 px/s, smoothstepped to a standstill at both ends); they now walk the car park to the doors at 7.6–15.2 px/s. T71/T72/T74/T75 (W25): the dish farm is real parabolic antennas built off a projected rim frame rather than grey ovals, the warehouse is a clad shed with a dock face, the container yard moved into the bottom-left corner and reads as containers, and the seating dropped to z 0.084–0.128 clear of both the road and the LAUNCH button. T69/T73 (W24): the crawler now runs one straight level line from the hold-down ring to the bay — W23_ROUTE is two points at the same z, so the ship holds scale 1 the whole way and the hand-overs with drawPadScene are exact by construction rather than by tuning. The main door is the whole pad-facing high bay. The ship is fuelled inside on the fuel beat: propellant hall, lagged transfer line, swing arm mated to the tank, frost, boil-off and a vent plume. Four platform levels, a control cabin, a parts rack, and much more through the building. T76: the base was alive during the rebuild and during the flight and dead in between, which is backwards — standing-ready is when you sit and look at it. Nothing scheduled a frame while phase === 'ready', so the site froze the instant the countdown ended. Idle runs its own loop now; the ladder's breathing ring gets every sixth frame because it costs a getBoundingClientRect. The rollout already read left to right. T78 turned the endgame into a cargo goal. It used to be a population target at 5 people per tonne, which is 81 launches at tier 10 and 236 at tier 8 — the last two thirds of the game were a grind. The base is now finished when BASE_CARGO_T (250 t, ten runs of a maxed ship) is landed, and population is a reading of that tonnage rather than a second running total, so the goal and the people can never disagree. Every strategy finishes the base in 10-11 launches. Nothing on screen counts launches; the player watches tonnes.
